explanation: Mixture of positions with no clear common thread: 'is'/'case' in fixed phrases like 'the same is true' / 'as the case may be', 'or' in boilerplate ('LICENSE_1_0.txt or copy at'), a later item in a list of places or names ('Florida, Texas,', 'New Hampshire'), plus assorted code tokens. Weak responses are scattered function words.

Fires on a heterogeneous set of tokens (the second part of compound identifiers like 'php[complete]', 'short[name]', 'Weak[Set]', 'access[_log]'; the second item in coordinated lists such as 'cardiac mortality', 'libm.a,'; numbers like '7 million'). No shared feature is apparent.

Fires on the word that introduces a variety or count of kinds: 'a' right after 'there are' ('there are a few/number of'), 'of' in 'types of', and 'different'/'separate'/'other'/'potential' after a numeral or quantifier ('three different', 'two separate', 'some other'). Plain articles without that 'several kinds of' sense give weak or no activation.

Mostly fires on a word-piece in the middle of a proper name, abbreviation or capitalized word ('PLA[INT]IFF', 'CIR[CU]IT', 'Flor[idian]', 'Kappa [Delta]', state code 'UT', 'T[2]0Is'), but a few top examples are ordinary English words ('reading', 'transferring', 'Assets'). The trigger is loose.

Fires on punctuation and operand tokens deep inside nested brackets in math (LaTeX) or code expressions: closing parentheses or braces, '(\', '+\', digits in fractions, and '[' / '],' in arrays and lambdas. It is strongest where several levels of bracketing are open; prose is near zero.

Fires on tokens in technical text about software performance, profiling and compiler/hardware settings: 'performance', 'benchmarks', 'CPU', 'GHz', '-O', '-m32', pragma/clang, timing code ('startTime', 'time.time()'). It also fires on whitespace or tokens inside such code. Generic code unrelated to speed or optimization is weak.

Fires on the digit inside a multi-digit number that is a quantity, measure or price (CSS '8px'/'10px', '90 overall', '£65', '360deg', '60 min'), usually the first or second digit after a space. Separately, it fires very strongly on the '=====' markdown underline beneath an 'Introduction' heading in papers.
Fires on Chinese or Japanese tokens, strongest inside code (string resources, comments, placeholders such as '请输入') and also in CJK prose. English tokens produce only weak, sporadic activation.

Fires on the empty-parentheses token '()' (including '().' and '()->') in function or method calls and definitions in code: 'main()', 'GetType()', 'set()', '@Input()'. Other empty bracket pairs ('[]', '{}', '{};') get moderate activation, and prose is near zero.

Fires loosely on the first token of a new sentence or clause that continues the discourse, especially a demonstrative or reference word ('This one', 'These frames', 'another', 'We', 'and'), plus a few content words just after such openings. The pattern is vague and many examples fit poorly.

Mainly fires on the capital 'K' (or 'k') that starts a proper name, especially a place name ('Kilkenny', 'Kettering', 'Kralingse', 'Kensington', 'KTV', 'de Kooning'). It also fires on 'at' before a venue name and on some unrelated code and technical tokens.

Mixed. It responds to words in license and boilerplate text ('Apache License', 'applicable law', 'set of attributes'), hyphens inside GUIDs or UUIDs, and a range of ordinary words in assorted prose ('burning', 'utilized', 'family', 'Perfect'). No single rule covers them.

Often fires on tokens inside all-caps legal case headings ('UNIT[ED] STATES', 'IN [THE] SUPERIOR COURT', 'WRIT [OF]', 'FACT [AND] OPINION'). It also fires on 'on' in news phrasing ('released on', 'arrested him on') and on scattered code and foreign-language tokens.

Fires on a grab-bag of tokens: 'new' ('the new password', 'new java.util.Date'), 'even', 'including' in patent claims ('a system including'), and boilerplate words ('copy of', 'OF THIS SOFTWARE'). No unifying context is evident.

Fires on function words (articles, prepositions, pronouns) and word pieces in running non-English European prose, especially German, then Spanish and French ('in den', 'en el', 'dizaines de'). It also fires on English articles in sports narration ('took a 21-', 'for a touchdown'). Technical English is weak.
No coherent pattern. Top examples span medical word pieces ('at[ax]ia', 'acid[uria]'), German dialogue, spacecraft 'orbit', JS callback args, author names and many unrelated words.

Fires on 'of' in court names in legal case captions ('Supreme Court of Oklahoma', 'Court of Appeals of Texas', 'OF TEXAS'). It also fires on the last digit of years and volumes in citation or category lines ('192[4] Summer Olympics', '12[6] Cal.App.'). Weaker activation comes from other legal-procedure words ('appeal to', 'writ of').

Mixed. It fires on word-initial or mid-word pieces, especially 'm' ('[m]olar', '[m]auling', '[m]ums'), name pieces ('Zel[az]ny'), and words in scientific abstracts ('results', 'studies', 'observations', 'may'). No single rule is evident.

A mixture: sentence-initial frequency or discourse adverbs ('Sometimes', 'Often', 'Consequently'), a closing parenthesis after a company or ticker ('(EDF)', 'INFO)'), company names followed by a verb ('Xiaomi Has', 'Flamingo has'), and 'any'/'a'/'in' in money or purchase contexts.

Fires on two things. (1) The first digits of a patent application or publication number after 'No.', 'JP', 'EP-A-' ('Japanese Patent Application No. 5[7]-...'). (2) A word-initial fragment of a multi-token word in non-English or Latin-root text ('[co]struzione', '[lo]yally', '[ra]ucous', '[co]-opted', '[for]ças').

No coherent pattern. Top examples include word pieces of bacterial names, 'in His name', '->prepare' in PHP database code, license words ('TORT', 'hereby', 'hope'), regex lookbehind and casual phrases ('what sort of').
